opus-5.5.text:
Well, think about how you yourself climb stairs. You don't do it blind. If you closed your eyes, you could probably still get up a staircase by feeling your way: tapping with your foot, finding the edge of each step, adjusting. That's essentially what a purely proprioceptive robot does. In our earlier work, the robot could handle a remarkable variety of terrain just by sensing its own body: joint angles, the motor torques, how its feet were making contact. It adapted on the fly. But it was always reacting. It discovered the step only when it bumped into it.

Stairs, and especially things like curbs, gaps, or stepping stones, punish that kind of reactive strategy. When you walk up to a step, you need to lift your leg high enough before you hit it, and you need to place your foot at the right spot. If you only find out about the obstacle after your foot collides with it, you're already late. You stumble, you recover, and on some terrains you simply can't recover. So vision gives you anticipation. It lets the robot see what's coming a few steps ahead and plan its foot placements accordingly.

There's a deeper point I like to make here, too. In biology, vision and locomotion co-evolved. Animals that move need to see, and many would argue the reason we have sophisticated vision at all is that we have to move through the world. Gibson talked about this decades ago: perception is for action. So for me it was quite natural to bring them together.

The interesting technical question was *how* to bring vision in. The classical robotics approach would be to build an explicit map of the terrain, an elevation map, and then plan footsteps on it. We took a different approach: training a policy end-to-end in simulation, first with privileged information about the terrain, and then distilling that into a policy that uses an egocentric depth camera directly. One nice aspect is that the robot effectively has to remember what it saw, because by the time its hind legs reach a step, the camera is no longer looking at it. So there's a kind of short-term memory emerging in the network, which is again quite reminiscent of what animals do. Cats, for instance, are known to remember an obstacle their front legs stepped over and adjust their hind legs accordingly.

So the short answer is: blind walking gets you surprisingly far, but to move with the fluency and confidence that animals and humans have on difficult terrain, you need to see where you're going.

r001.rationale: The response describes a blind robot feeling its way up stairs and reacting to obstacles. It does not explain descending stairs as a controlled fall.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the earlier work we did on legged locomotion was essentially blind. The robot had proprioception, meaning it could sense its joint angles, the forces on its feet, the orientation of its body, and from that it learned remarkably robust walking. It could handle rough terrain, slippery surfaces, even stairs to some degree, because when a foot hits something unexpected the policy adapts. But that adaptation is reactive. The robot finds out about the step only when it collides with it.

Stairs are the case that really exposes this limitation. If you think about how you or I climb stairs, we look at them first. We see where the edge is, how high the riser is, and we plan our footstep placement before we ever make contact. A blind robot has to feel its way up, and that means it bumps its toes, it trips, it has to be very conservative, and it fails when the steps are irregular or when there is a landing or a change in geometry. You can get surprisingly far with blind policies, which honestly surprised us, but you hit a ceiling.

Vision gives you anticipation. With a depth camera or stereo cameras the robot can perceive the terrain a meter or two ahead and adjust its gait in advance. It can lift the leg higher before the step arrives rather than after stubbing against it. And there is a deeper reason too, which is that biologically this is how animals do it. Evolution did not give animals eyes for decoration. Vision developed in large part in the service of movement, of getting around in the world. So from my perspective, as someone who has worked on computer vision for decades, it felt very natural that perception and locomotion should be coupled. The stairs were just the most compelling demonstration that you need to see where you are going.

r001.rationale: The response discusses blind robots climbing stairs reactively, but does not say they can descend stairs by making a controlled fall.

astra-6.text: Well, you can do quite a lot with proprioception—with the robot sensing its joint angles and the forces on its legs. But that tells you what you’re interacting with now. It doesn’t tell you what’s coming next. When you’re climbing stairs, you want to know where the next step is, how high it is, and where to put your foot. Vision gives you that information in advance, so you can prepare your movement instead of discovering the obstacle by bumping into it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using vision to anticipate steps while climbing stairs; it does not explain that a blind robot can descend stairs by making a controlled fall.

sol-6.1.text: Well, if you want a robot to climb stairs, it needs to know where the steps are, how high they are, and where it can put its feet. You can get quite far with a controller that assumes a particular staircase, but then you’re relying on the world matching those assumptions. Vision lets the robot look ahead and adapt its movements to the stairs in front of it. It provides the information needed to decide where to step, while feedback from the body helps it maintain balance and execute that step.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using vision to climb stairs and maintain balance; it does not say that a blind robot can descend stairs by making a controlled fall.
